title: Your chats on every device — round 7: catching up, the full relay, and hosting it yourself

steps.page: Catching up, and a full relay
steps.intro: How catch-up works: each device keeps a full copy of every chat and knows the last line it has. Whenever two of your devices are on at the same time, they compare every chat in the background, and whichever is ahead sends the other what it lacks. Any device can do this, not only the host. The relay stands in for a device that is asleep, for 48 hours after a chat's last line. After that, a device that missed lines simply waits for any of your devices that has them.

steps.path: The chat list on a device that missed lines
steps.headline: Should the relay keep a tiny note of how far each chat has got, so a device knows for certain when it is behind?
steps.today: Nothing tells a device whether its copy of a chat is the newest. The design so far could only say a device 'may' be behind.
steps.problem: After the 48 hours, the relay has deleted the lines. A phone opening that chat cannot tell whether it has everything or is missing two days of work, so every warning has to be vague.
steps.proposal: Yes means the relay keeps, with no time limit, one small note per chat: its latest line number and which device has it. No words of the chat. The phone can then say exactly: 'Desktop has 120 newer lines and is offline', and the chat list can mark that chat as waiting. No means the relay keeps nothing after 48 hours and warnings stay vague.

steps.surface: Continuing a chat on another device
steps.path: Continue here on a chat this device knows is behind
steps.headline: When a device knows it is behind and you tap Continue here anyway, what should happen?
steps.today: You chose 'allow, with a clear warning' for a device with no connection, where being behind is only possible. This is the case where it is certain.
steps.problem: Continuing from an older point while newer lines exist on a sleeping device is no longer an accident. It always produces two versions.
steps.proposal: You can always read the chat as far as this device has it. The choice is only about continuing.

options.label: Allow it, named honestly as a new version
pros: The button reads 'Continue from here as a new version', and the notice says Desktop's newer lines will stay as the other version.
You are never blocked from working.
Both versions are grouped in the resume browser, as you already decided for forks.
cons: You end up with two versions to tidy later.

options.label: Block until this device has caught up
pros: Two versions can never arise this way.
cons: If the desktop is asleep for a week, the chat cannot be continued anywhere for a week.

steps.path: Backup & Sync in settings, when the relay holds 1 GB for you
steps.headline: When the relay reaches your 1 GB limit, what should it let go of?
steps.today: The limit is agreed; what happens at the limit is not. The relay only holds lines and file changes that some device of yours has not received yet, so the limit is only reached while a device stays off during heavy work.
steps.problem: Something must give when the next line arrives and there is no room.
steps.proposal: Nothing is ever lost either way: your devices hold the full chats. This only decides which chats a returning device gets at once and which wait for another device to be on.

options.label: Release whole chats, least recently used first
pros: The chats you touched most recently are the ones a returning device gets straight away.
A chat is released whole, never left with a hole in the middle.
The host shows one line in Backup & Sync: 'Relay full. 3 older chats will reach Phone when both are on.' The phone marks those chats as waiting.
cons: An older chat can drop off the relay before its 48 hours are up.

options.label: Keep what is held, refuse new lines
pros: Simple; nothing already held is removed.
cons: Your newest work is exactly what a returning device would not get.

steps.path: A device that has not connected for a long time
steps.headline: Should the app offer to remove a device that has not been seen for 30 days?
steps.today: A device stays on the list forever. Removing one is manual.
steps.problem: A phone you sold or a laptop in a drawer makes the relay keep holding lines for it, and it still counts as trusted.
steps.proposal: Yes means a one-time prompt on your other devices: 'Old Laptop has not connected for 30 days. Remove it?' Nothing is removed unless you say so, and a removed device can be paired again. No means no prompt.

steps.intro: Why something in the middle exists at all: home internet and mobile data let your devices call out, but block calls coming in. Two devices that can each only call out cannot call each other; both must call the same place, which joins them. That place is the relay. It does not have to be ours. It can be a copy you run, or your own always-on device, provided that device can be reached from outside.

steps.path: A new kind of device in the Devices list
steps.headline: A super-host: a complete YouCoded with no window, doing everything our relay does and more, on hardware you control.
steps.changed: It pairs like any device. It keeps every chat and project in full with no time or size limit, hosts chats and runs replies itself, catches your other devices up, and passes live words between them. You can open it in a browser, as remote access works today.
steps.notice: It is one of your devices, so it holds your keys and can read your chats, unlike our relay, which cannot. That is the point of it, and why it must be hardware you trust.

steps.headline: Where should a super-host be able to live?
steps.today: Nothing like it exists on computers. YouCoded runs with no window only inside the phone app.
steps.problem: Where it lives decides whether your phone can reach it when you are away from home.
steps.proposal: Pick every place the design should support.

options.label: A device at home
pros: A desktop left on, a Mac mini or a Raspberry Pi. Nothing leaves your house.
A one-time cost of roughly $60 to $100 for a Pi, or nothing for a computer you already own.
cons: Reachable from outside only through a front door; the next question.

options.label: A small rented server
pros: Reachable from anywhere with no front door needed, so it fully replaces our relay.
About $2 to $6 a month, paid by the user to the hosting company.
cons: Your chats sit readable on a machine a hosting company owns.
Setup is more technical; the app would need a guided installer.

steps.path: Reaching a home super-host from outside
steps.headline: How should your phone reach a super-host at home when you are out?
steps.today: Remote access today works only through Tailscale.
steps.problem: A home device cannot receive calls from outside unless something gives it a front door.
steps.proposal: Pick every way the design should support. I recommend both: the first as the default, the second for users who want nothing of ours.

options.label: Through our relay, as a blind pipe
pros: No setup. The relay only passes locked traffic along and stores nothing, because your super-host does the storing.
cons: Still depends on our relay being up while you are away from home.

options.label: Your own front door, with a guided setup
pros: Nothing of ours involved at all. Choices include a free tunnel on your own Cloudflare account, Tailscale, or opening a port on your router.
This is what makes self-hosting fully equal to using ours.
cons: Each choice needs an account or router settings; some internet providers block the router method.
A tunnel or Tailscale is still somebody's service in the middle, though it is your account and it sees only locked traffic.

steps.path: Running your own copy of the relay
steps.headline: For users who want a blind relay of their own but no super-host, how should that copy be made?
steps.today: Our server is written for Cloudflare only. Its code is public, so anyone can put a copy on their own free Cloudflare account, but nowhere else.
steps.problem: You want hosting it yourself to be fully equal to using ours. If the two are built separately, the self-hosted one tends to fall behind.
steps.proposal: Either way the app gets a relay setting: YouCoded's, or an address of your own. A pairing code carries that address, so new devices need no typing.

options.label: Ours stays on Cloudflare; the app also contains its own relay, both held to one test
pros: Ours keeps costing nothing and needs no server upkeep from us.
Any super-host is automatically a relay too, with nothing extra to install.
A single set of checks must pass on both, which is what keeps them equal.
cons: Two builds of the same rules; a careless change could let one drift until the checks catch it.

options.label: One relay program everywhere, ours included
pros: Exactly equal by construction; what we run is what you run.
cons: We leave Cloudflare's free plan for a rented server: $2 to $6 a month from day one, and we must update and secure it ourselves.
One machine that can go down.

steps.path: Who pays for our relay, eventually
steps.headline: What principle should guide paying for our relay later?
steps.today: It is free and costs us nothing at today's size. The app has no payment system. Estimated cost is about 2 cents a month per heavy user past a few hundred users.
steps.problem: You said we cannot fund servers forever. The design should not paint us into a corner, even though no payment is being built now.
steps.proposal: This records a principle only. Self-hosting stays free and equal under every option.

options.label: Free at the basic limits; pay for bigger ones
pros: 48 hours and 1 GB stay free for everyone, so the app works out of the box.
A paid tier would buy a longer hold and more room, which is what actually costs us money.
cons: Needs a payment system one day, with company accounts and tax handling.

options.label: Free for everyone, supported by donations
pros: Simplest; no payment system.
cons: If donations fall short we carry the cost or tighten the limits for everyone.

options.label: Leave it open
pros: No commitment before real costs are measured.
cons: The limits may get designed without knowing which of them a paid tier would change.

steps.headline: Anything about catching up or self-hosting that is still unclear?
steps.today: Both of your comments on the design draft are answered in chat and on this deck.
steps.problem: If the explanation still does not land, the choices above rest on sand.
steps.proposal: Write anything, or leave it empty.
steps.prompt: e.g. I still do not see why two phones cannot just find each other
